candidate_relations.reason: The clinical picture—firm globular mass in vaginal canal with inability to identify cervical os or palpate uterine fundus, chronic bleeding, prior obstetric history, and normal ultrasound—is classic for uterine inversion. Vaginal sarcoma is a distinct malignant entity with no anatomical or pathophysiological overlap with uterine inversion.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Vaginal sarcoma is a primary malignant neoplasm of the vagina; uterine inversion is a structural/anatomical displacement of the uterus

candidate_relations.reason: Both conditions can present with a vaginal mass and bleeding, and the inability to palpate the uterine fundus is more consistent with inversion than prolapse. Uterine prolapse with ulceration is a related but incompatible structural diagnosis—in prolapse the cervical os is identifiable and the uterus is not inverted. The absence of an identifiable cervical os and non-palpable fundus point specifically to inversion, not prolapse.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Uterine prolapse involves descent of the uterus through the vaginal canal with the cervix/uterus remaining anatomically intact; uterine inversion involves fundal inversion through the cervix, a distinct anatomical state

case_quality_flags: Chronic uterine inversion (15-month history) is an uncommon presentation; normal pelvic ultrasound reports despite large vaginal mass suggest operator/equipment limitation rather than true absence of pathology
Absence of MRI limits definitive pre-operative anatomical characterization
